statement: To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.
heath_proof: Let AB, the diameter of the given sphere, be set out, and let it be cut at C so that AC is equal to CB, and at D so that AD is double of DB; let the semicircle AEB be described on AB, from C, D let CE, DF be drawn at right angles to AB, and let AF, FB, EB be joined. Then, since AD is double of DB, therefore AB is triple of BD. Convertendo, therefore, BA is one and a half times AD. But, as BA is to AD, so is the square on BA to the square on AF, [V. Def. 9, VI. 8] for the triangle AFB is equiangular with the triangle AFD; therefore the square on BA is one and a half times the square on AF. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. [XIII. 13] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore AF is equal to the side of the pyramid. Again, since AD is double of DB, therefore AB is triple of BD. But, as AB is to BD, so is the square on AB to the square on BF; [VI. 8, V. Def. 9] therefore the square on AB is triple of the square on BF. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also triple of the square on the side of the cube. [XIII. 15] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore BF is the side of the cube. And, since AC is equal to CB, therefore AB is double of BC. But, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BE; therefore the square on AB is double of the square on BE. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also double of the square on the side of the octahedron. [XIII. 14] And AB is the diameter of the given sphere; therefore BE is the side of the octahedron. Next, let AG be drawn from the point A at right angles to the straight line AB, let AG be made equal to AB, let GC be joined, and from H let HK be drawn perpendicular to AB. Then, since GA is double of AC, for GA is equal to AB, and, as GA is to AC, so is HK to KC, therefore HK is also double of KC. Therefore the square on HK is quadruple of the square on KC; therefore the squares on HK, KC, that is, the square on HC, is five times the square on KC. But HC is equal to CB; therefore the square on BC is five times the square on CK. And, since AB is double of CB, and, in them, AD is double of DB, therefore the remainder BD is double of the remainder DC. Therefore BC is triple of CD; therefore the square on BC is nine times the square on CD. But the square on BC is five times the square on CK; therefore the square on CK is greater than the square on CD; therefore CK is greater than CD. Let CL be made equal to CK, from L let LM be drawn at right angles to AB, and let MB be joined. Now, since the square on BC is five times the square on CK, and AB is double of BC, and KL double of CK, therefore the square on AB is five times the square on KL. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also five times the square on the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron has been described. [XIII. 16] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore KL is the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron has been described; therefore KL is a side of the hexagon in the said circle. [IV. 15] And, since the diameter of the sphere is made up of the side of the hexagon and two of the sides of the decagon inscribed in the same circle, [XIII. 16] and AB is the diameter of the sphere, while KL is a side of the hexagon, and AK is equal to LB, therefore each of the straight lines AK, LB is a side of the decagon inscribed in the circle from which the icosahedron has been described. And, since LB belongs to a decagon, and ML to a hexagon, for ML is equal to KL, since it is also equal to HK, being the same distance from the centre, and each of the straight lines HK, KL is double of KC, therefore MB belongs to a pentagon. [XIII. 10] But the side of the pentagon is the side of the icosahedron; [XIII. 16] therefore MB belongs to the icosahedron. Now, since FB is a side of the cube, let it be cut in extreme and mean ratio at N, and let NB be the greater segment; therefore NB is a side of the dodecahedron. [XIII. 17] And, since the square on the diameter of the sphere was proved to be one and a half times the square on the side AF of the pyramid, double of the square on the side BE of the octahedron and triple of the side FB of the cube, therefore, of parts of which the square on the diameter of the sphere contains six, the square on the side of the pyramid contains four, the square on the side of the octahedron three, and the square on the side of the cube two. Therefore the square on the side of the pyramid is fourthirds of the square on the side of the octahedron, and double of the square on the side of the cube; and the square on the side of the octahedron is one and a half times the square on the side of the cube. The said sides, therefore, of the three figures, I mean the pyramid, the octahedron and the cube, are to one another in rational ratios. But the remaining two, I mean the side of the icosahedron and the side of the dodecahedron, are not in rational ratios either to one another or to the aforesaid sides; for they are irrational, the one being minor [XIII. 16] and the other an apotome [XIII. 17]. That the side MB of the icosahedron is greater than the side NB of the dodecahedron we can prove thus. For, since the triangle FDB is equiangular with the triangle FAB, [VI. 8] proportionally, as DB is to BF, so is BF to BA. [VI. 4] And, since the three straight lines are proportional, as the first is to the third, so is the square on the first to the square on the second; [V. Def. 9, VI. 20] therefore, as DB is to BA, so is the square on DB to the square on BF; therefore, inversely, as AB is to BD, so is the square on FB to the square on BD. But AB is triple of BD; therefore the square on FB is triple of the square on BD. But the square on AD is also quadruple of the square on DB, for AD is double of DB; therefore the square on AD is greater than the square on FB; therefore AD is greater than FB; therefore AL is by far greater than FB. And, when AL is cut in extreme and mean ratio, KL is the greater segment, inasmuch as LK belongs to a hexagon, and KA to a decagon; [XIII. 9] and, when FB is cut in extreme and mean ratio, NB is the greater segment; therefore KL is greater than NB. But KL is equal to LM; therefore LM is greater than NB. Therefore MB, which is a side of the icosahedron, is by far greater than NB which is a side of the dodecahedron.
ai_proof_text:
13.18
**Statement:** To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere. Bisect AB at C [1.10], and cut off from AB its third part DB at D [6.9], so that AC = CB and AD = 2DB. With centre C and distance CA describe the semicircle AEB on AB [P3, D1.18]; C is its centre. From C and D draw CE and DF at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the semicircle at E and F, and join AF, FB, EB [P1].

**Step 2.** Since AD = 2DB, AB = AD + DB = 3DB [CN2]; and since AC = CB, AB = AC + CB = 2CB [CN2]. Further, AB = AD + DB where DB is half of AD, so AB is one and a half times AD.

**Step 3.** The angle AFB is in a semicircle, hence right [3.31]; and FD is drawn from the right angle perpendicular to the base AB. Therefore the triangles AFD, FBD are each similar to the whole triangle AFB [6.8], and from the equiangular triangles AFB, ADF and AFB, FDB we have BA : AF = AF : AD and AB : BF = BF : BD [6.4].

**Step 4.** Since BA, AF, AD are three proportional straight lines, BA has to AD the ratio duplicate of that which BA has to AF [D5.9], and the square on BA has to the square on AF that same duplicate ratio [6.20 por.]; hence BA : AD = sq(BA) : sq(AF). But BA is one and a half times AD [Step 2]; therefore sq(AB) is one and a half times sq(AF). Now the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid inscribed in that sphere [13.13]; therefore sq(AF) equals the square on the side of the pyramid, and AF is the side of the pyramid.

**Step 5.** Likewise, from AB : BF = BF : BD we get AB : BD = sq(AB) : sq(BF) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]; and AB = 3BD [Step 2], so sq(AB) = 3 sq(BF). The square on the diameter of the sphere is triple the square on the side of the cube inscribed in it [13.15]; therefore BF is the side of the cube.

**Step 6.** The angle AEB is right [3.31], and EC is the perpendicular from it to AB; so the triangles AEC, EBC are similar to AEB [6.8], whence AB : BE = BE : BC [6.4], and AB : BC = sq(AB) : sq(BE) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. Since AB = 2BC [Step 2], sq(AB) = 2 sq(BE). The square on the diameter of the sphere is double the square on the side of the octahedron inscribed in it [13.14]; therefore BE is the side of the octahedron.

**Step 7.** For the icosahedron: at A draw AG at right angles to AB [1.11], make AG = AB [1.3], and join GC [P1]. In triangle GAC the angle at A is right, so sq(CG) = sq(CA) + sq(AG) [1.47], which is greater than sq(CA) [CN5]; thus CG > CA, the radius, and G lies outside the circle. Since C is the centre, GC cuts the semicircle at a point H between G and C. From H draw HK perpendicular to AB [1.12]; K falls between A and C.

**Step 8.** The triangles GAC and HKC have the angle at C common and the angles at A and K right, hence equal [P4]; therefore their remaining angles AGC, KHC are equal [1.32], and the triangles are equiangular. Hence GA : AC = HK : KC [6.4]. But GA = AB = 2AC [Step 2]; therefore HK = 2KC [D5.5].

**Step 9.** Since HK = 2KC, the square on HK is four times the square on KC, the duplicate of the double ratio [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. And since the angle HKC is right, sq(HC) = sq(HK) + sq(KC) [1.47] = 5 sq(KC). But HC = CB, being radii of the same circle [D1.15]; therefore sq(BC) = 5 sq(CK).

**Step 10.** AB = 2CB and AD = 2DB [Steps 1, 2]; subtracting, the remainder DB is double of the remainder CB − DB = DC [CN3]. Hence BC = BD + DC = 3DC [CN2], so sq(BC) = 9 sq(DC) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. Therefore 9 sq(DC) = 5 sq(CK) [CN1]. Since 9 sq(DC) > 5 sq(DC) [CN5], 5 sq(CK) > 5 sq(DC), so sq(CK) > sq(CD) and CK > CD.

**Step 11.** On CB make CL = CK [1.3]; from L draw LM at right angles to AB, meeting the semicircle at M [1.11]; join MB [P1]. Since CL = CK > CD, L lies beyond D from A; AD is a part of AL, so AL > AD [CN5].

**Step 12.** AB = 2BC and KL = KC + CL = 2CK; therefore sq(AB) = 4 sq(BC) and sq(KL) = 4 sq(CK) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. And sq(BC) = 5 sq(CK) [Step 9]; therefore sq(AB) = 20 sq(CK) = 5 sq(KL).

**Step 13.** The square on the diameter of the sphere is five times the square on the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron is described [13.16 por.]. AB is that diameter; hence sq(KL) equals the square on that radius, and KL equals that radius, that is, KL is the side of the hexagon inscribed in that circle [4.15 por.].

**Step 14.** AC = CB and CK = CL; subtracting, AK = LB [CN3]. The diameter of the sphere is composed of the side of the hexagon and two sides of the decagon inscribed in that same circle [13.16 por.]; AB = AK + KL + LB, and KL is the side of the hexagon; therefore AK + LB is double the side of the decagon [CN3], and since AK = LB, each of AK, LB is the side of the decagon inscribed in that circle.

**Step 15.** In the right-angled triangles HKC, MLC, sq(HK) = sq(HC) − sq(CK) and sq(ML) = sq(MC) − sq(CL) [1.47]; HC = MC [D1.15] and CK = CL; therefore sq(HK) = sq(ML) [CN3] and HK = ML. But HK = 2KC = KL [Steps 8, 12]; therefore ML = KL [CN1], and ML is the side of the hexagon inscribed in the said circle.

**Step 16.** The angle MLB is right, so sq(MB) = sq(ML) + sq(LB) [1.47], that is, the squares on the side of the hexagon and the side of the decagon inscribed in the said circle. But the square on the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in a circle equals the squares on the sides of the hexagon and of the decagon inscribed in the same circle [13.10]. Therefore MB is the side of the pentagon inscribed in the circle from which the icosahedron is described; and the side of the icosahedron is the side of that pentagon [13.16]. Hence MB is the side of the icosahedron.

**Step 17.** For the dodecahedron: cut FB, the side of the cube, in extreme and mean ratio at N [6.30], NB being the greater segment. When the side of the cube is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the side of the dodecahedron [13.17 por.]. Therefore NB is the side of the dodecahedron. Thus AF, BE, BF, MB, NB have been set out as the sides of the pyramid, octahedron, cube, icosahedron and dodecahedron inscribed in the sphere of diameter AB.

**Step 18.** Comparison of the pyramid, octahedron and cube: sq(AB) is one and a half times sq(AF), double sq(BE), and triple sq(BF) [Steps 4, 5, 6]. Of the parts of which sq(AB) contains six, sq(AF) contains four, sq(BE) three, and sq(BF) two. Hence sq(AF) is four thirds of sq(BE), sq(AF) is double sq(BF), and sq(BE) is one and a half times sq(BF). The squares on AB, AF, BE, BF are all measured by the same area, so these lines are commensurable in square [D10.1.2], and the sides of the pyramid, octahedron and cube are in rational ratios to one another and to the diameter. Also, since four parts exceed three and three exceed two, AF > BE > BF [CN5]; and NB, a part of BF, is less than BF [CN5].

**Step 19.** Let the diameter AB be the rational straight line set out [D10.1.3]. Then MB, the side of the icosahedron, is the irrational straight line called minor [13.16], and NB, the side of the dodecahedron, is the irrational straight line called apotome [13.17]; each is incommensurable with AB both in length and in square [D10.1.3]. Since sq(AF), sq(BE), sq(BF) are commensurable with sq(AB) [Step 18] while sq(MB), sq(NB) are incommensurable with sq(AB), sq(MB) and sq(NB) are incommensurable with each of sq(AF), sq(BE), sq(BF) [10.13]. Thus the sides of the icosahedron and of the dodecahedron are irrational lines of different species, and neither is in a rational ratio to the sides of the other three figures.

**Step 20.** It remains to show that MB > NB. sq(AB) = 3 sq(BF) [Step 5], and AB = 3DB gives sq(AB) = 9 sq(DB) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]; so 3 sq(BF) = 9 sq(DB) [CN1] and sq(BF) = 3 sq(DB). Since AD = 2DB, sq(AD) = 4 sq(DB) [D5.9, 6.20 por.], which is greater than 3 sq(DB) = sq(BF) [CN5]; so AD > FB. And AL > AD [Step 11]; therefore AL > FB.

**Step 21.** AK is the side of the decagon and KL the side of the hexagon inscribed in the same circle [Steps 13, 14]; therefore AL = AK + KL is cut in extreme and mean ratio at K with KL its greater segment [13.9], so AL : KL = KL : AK [D6.3], and rect(AL, AK) = sq(KL) [6.17]. Likewise FB : NB = NB : NF [D6.3], and rect(FB, NF) = sq(NB) [6.17].

**Step 22.** KL > NB. For if NB were not less than KL, then, AL being greater than FB [Step 20], NF = FB − NB would be less than AL − KL = AK; thus rect(FB, NF), having both its sides less than the corresponding sides of rect(AL, AK), would be a part of it and less than it [CN5]; that is, sq(NB) < sq(KL) and NB < KL, contrary to the supposition. Hence KL > NB.

**Step 23.** ML = KL [Step 15]; therefore ML > NB. The angle MLB is right, so sq(MB) = sq(ML) + sq(LB) [1.47], which is greater than sq(ML) [CN5]; thus MB > ML, and therefore MB > NB. So the side MB of the icosahedron is greater than the side NB of the dodecahedron; and the sides of the five figures have been set out and compared with one another. Q.E.F.
